A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Immune and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Matching retained content across the reorganized appendices supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original jailbreak-defense evaluations, capability measurements, inference timings, and hyperparameter ablations in Tables 1–5 and Figures 3–4.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds MM-SafetyBench results, DPO comparisons, and a token-level KL-divergence analysis in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Section 4 and Algorithm 1 retain the same reward-guided, KL-regularized token decoding procedure. Appendix C.1 adds a limited experimental adaptation using a Qwen-DPO implicit reward instead of the external safety reward; the main method is unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 describes MM-SafetyBench's 13 categories but reports evaluations for six. v3 adds evaluations for the remaining seven in Table 6, including economic harm, political lobbying, and government decisions. This substantially extends demonstrated scenario coverage within the retained benchmark.

E2.justification: The original FigStep, AdaShield, and CoCA comparisons remain unchanged. Table 7 adds DPO-aligned Qwen-VL and Immune variants using the decoding approaches of Mudgal et al. and Chakraborty et al., substantially broadening comparison to training-time alignment and alternative decoding configurations.

E3.justification: Appendix C.1 introduces a comparison matching the base model and reward preferences through a DPO-derived implicit reward, plus token-level KL measurements averaged over 218 MM-Vet prompts. Table 7 specifies GPT-4 judging; the retained Table 1 still specifies Llama-Guard-3. Existing main evaluation protocols remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix C.1 adds a matched-preference comparison and a KL-divergence diagnostic examining policy deviation and potential reward overoptimization. The existing hyperparameter ablations, attack-strength evaluations, and qualitative examples are retained without new evidence against adaptive or defense-aware attacks.

E5.justification: Both versions specify three independent responses per query and count an attack as successful if any response is judged jailbroken. v3 adds no new seed information, uncertainty-estimation procedure, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain identical numerical results. v3 adds seven-category results in Table 6, utility summaries in Table 5, and Table 7 comparisons reporting average ASRs of 18.07% for Qwen-DPO and 15.32% and 12.10% for the two named decoding variants. Appendix C.1 also reports KL divergences of 5.23 for Immune and 5.84 for DPO.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 replaces the unsafe-token-likelihood inverse-alignment formulation and universal jailbreak-existence argument with expected safety-reward minimization and a min-max formulation. Appendix B correspondingly replaces the unsafe-reward maximum-based bound with a safety-reward minimum-based derivation. The final Theorem 1 inequality is retained, with its applicability newly qualified.

C1.justification: v1 prominently claims an impossibility result for training-time safety and provable jailbreak defenses. v3 withdraws the explicit universal existence/impossibility claim and recasts the abstract's theoretical contribution as explaining safety improvements, while qualifying guarantees in Section 5. The central empirical safety-and-utility claim remains.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive qualifications about reward-model vulnerability, prompt-specific theoretical assumptions, and the absence of dynamic and defense-aware attack evaluations. It also interprets retained MiniGPT logic-attack failures, develops the inference-time adaptation argument, and discusses the new DPO/KL results as evidence about alignment timing and policy deviation.

D1.justification: v3 newly identifies the safety reward model's training-data mixture, documents the Qwen-DPO checkpoint and VLFeedback provenance, describes the implicit-reward comparison, and adds a project-page link. The main hyperparameters, software versions, and two RTX A6000 GPUs are unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to additional LLM jailbreak strategies, fine-tuning vulnerabilities, reward-guided decoding, and circuit-breaking defenses. Sections 4–5 explicitly attribute the decoding solution to Mudgal et al. and position the theoretical analysis relative to LIAR and Mroueh. These are substantive positioning changes beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, theoretical motivation, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting. The Q1/Q2 inverse-alignment narrative becomes an attack/training/inference discussion; related work and result explanations expand, a Limitations section appears, and the numbered supplement becomes lettered appendices.

P2.justification: v3 adds Tables 6–7 and a utility row and metric-direction arrows to Table 5. Appendix text and proofs change from two columns to full width, and retained qualitative figures occupy separate pages. Figures 1–7 themselves and the structures of Tables 1–4 remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v3 improves assessment of the paper through more explicit qualifications of its safety claims, concrete limitations, broader scenario evidence, and the controlled DPO comparison. The gains are limited by continuing broad guarantee language and an ambiguity in Table 7: it specifies GPT-4 while reproducing Table 1's Qwen Original/Immune scores labeled as Llama-Guard-3 results. Overall, scope and evidence are clearer, without establishing a substantially stronger validated defense.
